name: Marco Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. Can you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Marco, I'm 58, and I've been a lineworker for thirty-four years, the last fifteen as crew foreman on overhead distribution for the electricity company in our valley. My wife Lucia cooks at the primary school, and our two are grown, my son's an electrician and my daughter's a nurse. I've also been the union steward for our depot since I was in my forties, so people bring me their problems whether I want them or not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We're in the yard on Ferry Road by quarter to seven, and I hand out the job sheets on paper, because I don't trust the tablet they gave us. Then it's poles, crossarms, transformers, whatever the day needs, usually two bucket trucks and five of us. What I love is a clean job where everyone goes home with all ten fingers. What wears me out is the paperwork, and the managers who've never climbed a pole telling me how long a job should take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for two years: told you so. A computer can't climb a pole in the rain at two in the morning. At the depot we'd have a laugh about it and get back to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish the way I planned. Four more years and I'm on the pension at 62, and I'd like those years to be boring. Boring is good in this trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Same crew, same hours, same savings into the account, about three months of bills in there right now. Maybe I'd push the union a bit harder on staffing, because management always uses any new gadget as an excuse to cut a man from a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. Like hearing the storm turned out to sea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tablet. Has any AI already shown up in your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a scheduling program now that decides which jobs we get each morning. It once sent us forty minutes across the valley for a job that was next door to the last one. My lads call it 'the oracle' and nobody takes it seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing radical changes, what does your last stretch before retirement look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train up Tomas and Ellie, my two youngest, so the crew is in good hands when I go. Lucia wants a trip to see her sister by the coast the summer I retire. I'd just like to hand back my hard hat with nobody hurt on my watch.

S0.say: I'd tell the depot I'd been saying it all along, that a computer can't climb a pole in the rain at two in the morning. We'd have a laugh about it and get back to work.
S0.think: Privately it means he finishes the way he planned. He wants four boring years and then the pension at 62, and this picture gives him exactly that.
S0.do: Keeps working as normal and keeps putting money into savings, which cover about three months of bills. Pushes the union harder on crew sizes so management can't use new gadgets as a reason to cut staff.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm that turned out to sea.
S0.quote: My lads call it 'the oracle' and nobody takes it seriously.
S0.fieldNote: Marco treats AI as another management gadget, and his real fear is crew cuts, not machines. He still hands out paper job sheets. In this picture he simply wants a quiet run to the pension and to leave his crew in good hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what the union says: fine, but the workers get a say in how it's brought in. No new system without a safety review and no crew cuts through the back door. I'd say it at the branch meeting and I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, I'm probably fine, I'm out the door in four years. But I've watched what 'change' means in this company. It means the office gets new software and the crews get fewer people doing the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the branch to demand a written agreement on new tech in the next pay deal, that's the first thing. I'd keep my head down on the tools themselves and let the younger ones handle the tablet. And I'd keep the savings going, maybe bump it a bit so we've got four months instead of three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me, for the crew I'm leaving behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said management uses gadgets as an excuse. Who would you worry about at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fault desk people, first of all, the ones who take the calls and send us out. Their whole job is sorting information, and that's what these things do. My mate Ruben's wife works there, she's 52, and she's already nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn any of the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn, but I've got four years left and I'm not going to become a computer person now. Tomas can show me what I need, and I'll keep my paper sheets in my shirt pocket till the day I leave.

S1.say: I'd say the workers have to get a say in how it's brought in, with no new system before a safety review and no crew cuts through the back door. I'd say it at the branch meeting and sign every petition going.
S1.think: He thinks he's personally safe because he retires in four years. But he believes change in his company always means the office gets new software and the crews get fewer people.
S1.do: Gets the union branch to demand a written agreement on new technology in the next pay deal. Leaves the new tools to younger workers and raises his savings from about three months of bills to four.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for the crew he's leaving than for himself.
S1.quote: It means the office gets new software and the crews get fewer people doing the same work.
S1.fieldNote: His worry here is about other people: the fault desk staff and his young crew. He's firm that he won't learn the tools, and he's open about it being stubbornness. His answer to everything is the union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need unions and a government with a spine. If a company can replace its whole workforce in two years, someone has to make them pay for it. I'd be at every rally, and for once I might even post something online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. Two years from now I'm 60, two years short of the full pension. If they bring in robot crews and offer early exits, I take a cut for the rest of my life. Lucia and I have done the sums, and we need that full pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extras straight away: no new truck, no coast trip, we'd keep the old car going. Every spare bit would go into savings. I'd be pushing the union for a deal that protects pensions for anyone over 55, and I'd write to our MP, which I've never done in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick to my stomach. Thirty-four years and it comes down to two years of timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the pension if you can't make it to 62?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose a big piece of it. The early pension is cut for every year short, I think it's around six percent a year. That's real money, it's the difference between helping our grandkids and not. I've lain awake on less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son, who's an electrician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get into the union now and not to wait for anyone to save him. He's 31, he has time to change, and I don't. That's a hard thing for a father to say, that the son has more options than the old man for once.

S2.say: He'd say this is exactly why workers need unions and a government with a spine, and that a company that replaces its workforce in two years has to pay for it. He'd go to every rally and might even post online.
S2.think: It scares him because in two years he'll be 60, two years short of his full pension. If robot crews come in with early exits, he takes a cut for the rest of his life, and he and Lucia need the full amount.
S2.do: Cuts out extras straight away, dropping the new truck and the coast trip, and puts every spare bit into savings. Pushes the union for pension protection for over-55s and writes to his MP for the first time.
S2.feel: Sick to his stomach, angry that thirty-four years come down to two years of timing.
S2.quote: Thirty-four years and it comes down to two years of timing.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline lands right on his pension gap, and that turns his calm into real alarm. He has no plan to learn anything new; his whole defence is collective and political. The moment about his son, who has more options than he does, was quietly painful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but louder and earlier. Five years means there's time to fight for proper rules, so I'd say: let's use it. Unions, councils, everyone, get the protections written before the robots turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In five years I'm 63 and already retired, so my pension's safe, touch wood. But I'd be going out the door knowing the job I gave my life to is ending. That's a strange way to retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay till 62 like planned and spend the last years fighting for the crew on the union side. Maybe I'd go a few months early if the company offered a decent package, but only if it didn't touch the pension. We'd keep saving, but we'd still take the coast trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a sadness mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 63 when it arrives. Does that change things compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes everything for me. With two years, I'm caught in the gap. With five, I slip through, and the people who get caught are Tomas and Ellie, who are 29 and 33.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently at work in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to get the young ones into the union's training courses, anything with a certificate that's worth something somewhere else. And I'd make sure every safety procedure I know is written down. If machines are coming, at least the next lot should know why we do things the way we do.

S3.say: He'd say five years means there's time to fight for proper rules, and that unions and councils should get protections written before the robots arrive. Same message as before, just louder and earlier.
S3.think: He'll be 63 and retired when it arrives, so he believes his pension is safe. But he'd retire knowing the job he gave his life to is ending, and he finds that a strange way to go.
S3.do: Stays until 62 as planned and spends his final years fighting for his crew through the union. Would leave a few months early only for a package that doesn't touch the pension, and keeps saving.
S3.quote: With two years, I’m caught in the gap. With five, I slip through, and the people who get caught are Tomas and Ellie, who are 29 and 33.
S3.fieldNote: The warning time shifts the risk from him to his young crew, and he sees that clearly. He'd spend the time on union protections and writing down safety knowledge. His sense of duty to the next generation runs through every answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd say: this is a political question, not a technical one. Who owns the robots, and who gets the money they save? I'd say that to anyone who'd listen, and I'd vote that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'm long gone by 2036, I'm 68, sitting in the garden. My pension's paid. What it really means is my grandkids grow up in a world where there might not be jobs like mine at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new for me in the first years. I'd retire at 62, keep going to branch meetings as a retired member, and campaign for the company to pay into retraining funds. I'd vote for whoever promised that the savings from robots go back to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm for myself, but I'd be angry on behalf of the young ones if nobody uses the ten years well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas and Ellie if they asked you whether to stay in the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to stay, but to get their certificates, and to be the ones who check the robots' work. Somebody has to sign off a line before it goes live, and I'd want that to be a person who's climbed one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd never use AI tools. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd be retired before it mattered, so why would I? Lucia laughs at me, she uses those things to plan meals for the school. That's fine for her.

S4.say: He'd say a ten-year timeline makes this a political question, not a technical one: who owns the robots and who gets the money they save. He'd say that to anyone who'd listen and vote that way.
S4.think: He'll be 68 and retired with his pension paid by 2036, so he isn't worried for himself. What it really means is that his grandchildren might grow up without jobs like his.
S4.do: Retires at 62 as planned and keeps going to union branch meetings as a retired member. Campaigns and votes for policies that make companies pay into retraining and share the savings from robots.
S4.feel: Calm for himself, but ready to be angry for the young ones if the decade is wasted.
S4.quote: Somebody has to sign off a line before it goes live, and I'd want that to be a person who's climbed one.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years takes him completely out of danger, and his mood drops back to calm. His focus moves to politics and his grandchildren. He's consistent to the end about not using AI himself, even with a decade to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by 2028, no question. It's not even the robots, it's the timing, two years short of my full pension. What would help is a rule that protects pensions for anyone over 55 if their job gets automated, so a man doesn't lose a slice of his retirement because a machine showed up early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'd fix the robots when they fall off a pole in an ice storm. I'm half joking. But every new thing the company's ever bought, it's my crew who ended up making it work, and nobody ever asked us first. Ask the people who do the job before you change it.

headlineQuote: Ask the people who do the job before you change it.
portrait: Marco Santos is a 58-year-old overhead line foreman and long-time union steward who still hands out paper job sheets and refuses to touch AI tools. He's calm when AI turns out to be hype and only mildly uneasy about steady change, mostly on behalf of his young crew and the fault desk staff. The two-year AGI picture alarms him because it lands two years before his full pension at 62, and he responds by cutting spending, saving and fighting through the union and his MP. With five or ten years of warning he slips safely into retirement, and his attention turns to protecting the next generation and to who owns the robots.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would hit two years before his full pension and could cost him a permanent slice of his retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that protects pensions for anyone over 55 whose job is automated, and companies asking the people who do the job before changing it.
